correctness.rationale: The neutral component is the split diagonal algebra, so a component-permuting algebra automorphism permutes its primitive idempotents. One-dimensional corners then force each matrix unit to map to a nonzero scalar multiple of a uniquely permuted matrix unit. Matrix-unit multiplication gives the cocycle equation c_xy c_yz=c_xz, solved by c_xy=d_x d_y^{-1}; hence the scalar factor is exactly (k^×)^G/k^×. The degree equation sigma(x)^{-1}sigma(y)=pi(x^{-1}y) yields sigma(x)=a pi(x) and pi(xg)=pi(x)pi(g), so pi is a group automorphism and sigma is left-affine. Every such affine permutation and diagonal conjugation works, proving both semidirect products and the quotient. The checker independently verifies the affine classification for C2, C3, C4, V4 and S3. No finite experiment is used as an infinite proof.

residual_risks: Older literature on automorphisms of group gradings or normalizers of crossed-product gradings may contain the same holomorph formula under different terminology.

The componentwise permutation subgroup itself is not new: it is already identified with G in arXiv:1607.03942v1. The originality claim is restricted to the full component-permuting group, diagonal extension, and Weyl quotient.

value.rationale: The recent classification isolates a unique extremal strong strictly elementary matrix grading for each finite group. Computing its complete internal symmetry is a natural structural invariant, not an arbitrary parameter slice: it separates degree-preserving symmetries from weak component permutations and identifies the Weyl quotient exactly with Aut(G). The formula applies uniformly to nonabelian groups and arbitrary fields and gives exact finite-field automorphism counts. This provides a concrete symmetry layer absent from the classification theorem itself.
